text:
**Short answer:** Yes, at about $450-$475 or less, if you mostly run AC appliances for outages or car camping. At $499 or more, newer models are a better buy.

**What it offers**
- It has a 1,152Wh LiFePO4 battery rated for 3,500+ cycles, 1,800W AC output (2,700W surge), and a 5-year warranty ([Bluetti](https://www.bluettipower.com/products/ac180?variant=44099774480603)).
- Real-world capacity is good. Six independent tests found about 991Wh usable, or 86% of rated ([Watt Power Station](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/)). PCWorld measured 84-87% AC efficiency ([PCWorld](https://www.pcworld.com/article/1966571/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review.html)).
- It charges fast, about 1.3 hours from empty on a wall outlet ([OutdoorGearLab](https://www.outdoorgearlab.com/reviews/camping-and-hiking/power-station/bluetti-ac180)).

**Drawbacks**
- It's heavy for its capacity, at about 36 lb, and the fan is audible while charging ([OutdoorGearLab](https://www.outdoorgearlab.com/reviews/camping-and-hiking/power-station/bluetti-ac180)).
- It's inefficient on small loads. At about 34W, one test got only 54% of rated capacity, which matters for a CPAP or an overnight fridge ([Watt Power Station](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/)).
- DC efficiency was only 71% in PCWorld's test, so it's weaker for USB-heavy use ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review-excellent-ac-efficiency-but-heavy-and-less-impressive-over-dc/)).
- The 2,700W "Power Lifting" mode only works for resistive heating loads, and not while charging from the wall ([Best Batteries](https://us.best-batteries.com/reviews/bluetti-ac180/)).
- The sources disagree on expansion. Bluetti's page advertises expansion batteries, but Watt Power Station says Bluetti's own FAQ says the AC180 isn't expandable. Check with Bluetti before buying if that matters to you.
- Some pages show discontinuation signals, so confirm stock and exact variant before you order ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review-excellent-ac-efficiency-but-heavy-and-less-impressive-over-dc/)).

**Newer alternatives at similar prices**
- OutdoorGearLab scored the AC180 a middling 66 and calls its successor, the Bluetti Elite 100 V2, "much improved": 25 lb, quieter, faster charging, with 1,024Wh instead of 1,152Wh. It also recommends the Anker Solix C1000 Gen 2 over the AC180 ([OutdoorGearLab](https://www.outdoorgearlab.com/reviews/camping-and-hiking/power-station/bluetti-ac180)).
- Watt Power Station lists the Elite 100 V2 at $489, the Anker C1000 Gen 2 at $499.99, and the EcoFlow Delta 3 Classic at $499, with 93% measured efficiency ([comparison](https://wattpowerstation.com/power-stations/bluetti-ac180/)).

**Where to buy**
- [Bluetti US store](https://www.bluettipower.com/products/ac180?variant=44099774480603): $499, with a 30-day price match.
- [Via Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/go/bluetti-ac180): the site's tested code AFF5OFF takes it to $474.05 (last tested Oct 21). This is an affiliate link that earns Dealectric a commission, and the store's checkout has the final word on the code.
- iTechGuides' Amazon listing showed $449 on Oct 24, but I don't have a direct link to it. Prices vary by variant, so check the listing yourself ([iTechGuides](https://www.itechguides.com/bluetti-ac180-power-station-review-excellent-ac-efficiency-but-heavy-and-less-impressive-over-dc/)).

If you tell me how you'd use it (outages, camping, CPAP, RV), I can say whether the AC180 or one of the newer models fits better.
